Build an interactive 2D figure from the brief below and the source image.

AUTHORED FIGURE BRIEF:
This figure stacks two ray-tracing constructions, panel (a) for a concave mirror and panel (b) for a convex mirror, each drawn in cross section with the mirror as a pale curved arc on the right. In (a) a red upward arrow at the far left is labeled Object, its base P resting on the horizontal optical axis and its tip Q above; the axis also carries the points C, P prime, F, and the vertex V. Four color-coded rays numbered 1 through 4 leave Q: ray 1 in blue runs parallel to the axis and reflects back through F, ray 2 in red arrives along a line through F and leaves parallel to the axis, ray 3 in purple heads toward C and returns along itself with a small right-angle square at the mirror, and ray 4 in green strikes V and reflects symmetrically across the axis. All four cross at Q prime, the tip of a short red downward arrow labeled Image whose base P prime lies between C and F, and a small drawn eye at the lower left looks toward the mirror. Panel (b) repeats the construction on a convex mirror whose focal point F and center of curvature C lie behind the arc: the reflected rays spread apart, and their dashed backward extensions meet at Q prime, tip of a smaller upright red arrow labeled Image standing behind the mirror between V and F. Pairing the panels contrasts rays that genuinely converge with an image sitting only where extensions cross.

REQUESTED INTERACTIONS:
- Toggle between concave mirror and convex mirror: learner switches the named mirror type; the reflected rays either meet in front of the mirror or spread while dashed backward extensions meet behind it; the difference between real and virtual image formation becomes clear.
- Click on principal ray 1, 2, 3, or 4: learner selects one numbered ray; that ray brightens from object tip to mirror and along its reflected or extended path; the specific ray rule behind each construction is isolated from the busy crossing diagram.
- Slider for object distance from the mirror: learner moves the object along the optical axis; the image arrow shifts, flips, and changes size for the concave case while the convex image stays upright and virtual; the relationship among object position, focal point, and image character becomes clear.

SOURCE FILE: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 35: Geometric Optics and Image Formation

There is no blueprint: decide the figure type, elements, labels, controls, and any step sequence yourself.
